## The core difference

**Merge** creates a new commit that ties two branches together. Both histories remain intact in the final history.

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of another branch and rewrites the commit hashes. Your work appears to have been built on top of the latest state, but it didn't happen that way.

## How they look

**Merge:**
```
main:    A—B—C———————D
              ╲       ╱
feature:       E—F—G
```
The history shows the branch existed and when it rejoined. Reading the commit log shows the shape of the work.

**Rebase:**
```
main:    A—B—C
feature:       C—E'—F'—G'
```
The commits E, F, G get replayed as E', F', G' (new hashes). History looks linear. A reader doesn't see when feature work started relative to main.

## When to use each

**Use merge when:**
- The branch is shared or already pushed (rewriting history breaks other people's clones)
- You want to see when the work was integrated (useful for reading release history)
- The branch represents a logical unit of work that should stay grouped (feature branches, release branches)
- Multiple people are working on the branch and will push again

**Use rebase when:**
- The branch is local-only or you're the sole owner
- You want a clean, linear history (easier to `git log`, easier to bisect)
- You're syncing with main before a PR (getting latest main code without a merge commit noise)
- You're cleaning up your own work before pushing

## The trade-offs

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| **History** | Shows when work was done, in what order | Linear, clean-looking, harder to trace timing |
| **Conflict resolution** | Done once, in the merge commit | Done per-commit as they're replayed (tedious for multi-commit) |
| **Recovery** | Easy—the old branch still exists | Hard—old commits are orphaned, need reflog |
| **Team safety** | Safe; never rewrites shared history | Dangerous if pushed; breaks other clones |
| **Bisect / blame** | Shows integration point | Shows original authorship without integration noise |

## Recommendation

- **Local work before pushing:** rebase onto main, push once. Linear, clean.
- **Shared work, PR review:** merge the PR. The merge commit is documentation.
- **Syncing repeatedly during development:** rebase each time you pull main, but only before you've pushed.
- **Undoing a mistake:** use merge. If you rebased and pushed, you've now got a mess to untangle across the team.

The rule many teams follow: rebase locally, merge to main. That way main stays clean and linear, but your PR history shows nothing was rewound.
